title: In a compacted topic, when and why does data "disappear" even though compaction retains the latest value per key — (1) a tombstone (null value) marks the key for deletion and after `delete.retention.ms` it's removed completely, (2) if `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` BOTH compaction AND time/size retention apply so even the latest record can expire, (3) messages with null or wrong keys bypass compaction entirely and are subject to retention deletion, (4) aggressive compaction settings (small segment size + frequent cleaner runs) remove old records almost immediately — and why is each of these expected behavior, not a bug?
shortTitle: In a compacted topic, when and why does data "disappear" even though compaction keeps the latest value per key?

s1_definition.profdef: Log compaction promises to retain at least the latest value per key, but that promise has well-defined exceptions, so data can legitimately disappear. A tombstone, a record with a null value, marks a key for deletion and is itself removed after the delete retention window, erasing the key entirely. If the cleanup policy is compact plus delete, ordinary time or size retention applies on top of compaction, so even the latest record for a key can expire. Records with a null key, or keyed incorrectly, are not compactable at all and are subject to plain retention deletion. And aggressive compaction settings, such as small segments and frequent cleaner runs, remove superseded records almost immediately. Each of these is the documented behavior of compaction, not a defect.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one current notice per account on a board, and the rule is "always keep the newest notice for each account." People expect nothing ever vanishes, but four documented rules say otherwise. First, if a clerk pins a blank "cancelled" slip for Rajesh and a day passes, even that cancelled slip is removed, so Rajesh's account vanishes from the board completely. Second, if the board also has a "nothing older than seven days" rule, then even Rajesh's newest notice disappears once it is seven days old. Third, notices pinned without an account number written on them cannot be matched to any account, so the "keep newest per account" rule does not apply to them and they are simply thrown out on the age rule. Fourth, if the tidy-up crew is told to work constantly and aggressively, old superseded notices for an account are pulled almost the instant a newer one is pinned. None of these is the board malfunctioning; they are exactly the rules as written.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compaction keeps the latest value per key, but tombstones expire the key after delete.retention.ms, compact,delete adds time or size expiry to even the latest record, null or wrong keys are not compactable and get retention-deleted, and aggressive settings purge old records almost instantly — all expected, all documented.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Log compaction promises to retain at least the latest value per key, but that promise has well-defined exceptions, so data can legitimately disappear. A tombstone, a record with a null value, marks a key for deletion and is itself removed after the delete retention window, erasing the key entirely. If the cleanup policy is compact plus delete, ordinary time or size retention applies on top of compaction, so even the latest record for a key can expire. Records with a null key, or keyed incorrectly, are not compactable at all and are subject to plain retention deletion. And aggressive compaction settings, such as small segments and frequent cleaner runs, remove superseded records almost immediately. Each of these is the documented behavior of compaction, not a defect.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps one current notice per account on a board, and the rule is "always keep the newest notice for each account." People expect nothing ever vanishes, but four documented rules say otherwise. First, if a clerk pins a blank "cancelled" slip for Rajesh and a day passes, even that cancelled slip is removed, so Rajesh's account vanishes from the board completely. Second, if the board also has a "nothing older than seven days" rule, then even Rajesh's newest notice disappears once it is seven days old. Third, notices pinned without an account number written on them cannot be matched to any account, so the "keep newest per account" rule does not apply to them and they are simply thrown out on the age rule. Fourth, if the tidy-up crew is told to work constantly and aggressively, old superseded notices for an account are pulled almost the instant a newer one is pinned. None of these is the board malfunctioning; they are exactly the rules as written.

**One line to remember:** Compaction keeps the latest value per key, but tombstones expire the key after delete.retention.ms, compact,delete adds time or size expiry to even the latest record, null or wrong keys are not compactable and get retention-deleted, and aggressive settings purge old records almost instantly — all expected, all documented.

sections.s2_technical:
Reason one is the tombstone. In a compacted topic, you delete a key by producing a record with that key and a null value, which is the tombstone. Compaction keeps the tombstone long enough for consumers to observe the delete, specifically for at least `delete.retention.ms`, which defaults to twenty-four hours. After that window and a subsequent cleaning pass, the tombstone itself is removed, and at that point the key is completely gone from the log, including any trace that it ever existed. So if you look for a key after its tombstone has aged out, the data has disappeared, and that is precisely the designed behavior: the tombstone is a self-expiring delete marker. You produce it like this:

```java
producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("account.profiles", "SAV2001", null)); // tombstone
// after delete.retention.ms + a cleaning pass, SAV2001 is fully gone
```

Reason two is the combined cleanup policy. A topic with `cleanup.policy=compact` only compacts and never expires the latest value per key. But a topic with `cleanup.policy=compact,delete` applies both compaction and ordinary time or size retention. That means a record can be removed because it is older than `retention.ms` or because the partition exceeded `retention.bytes`, even if it is the latest value for its key. People who assume a compacted topic keeps the latest value forever are surprised when the latest value for a rarely updated key expires purely on age. This combination is useful for things like a changelog that you want deduplicated by key but also bounded in time, and the expiry of a stale latest value is the intended effect, not a loss.

Reason three is non-compactable records. Compaction is keyed: it reasons about the latest record per key. A record with a null key has no key to deduplicate on, so compaction simply skips it, and such records are only ever removed by ordinary retention if the topic allows deletion, or they linger. Worse, if a producer accidentally sends records with the wrong key or a null key when you expected a real key, those records are not protected by the latest-per-key guarantee at all, so they can vanish under retention while you assumed compaction was keeping them. This is why discipline about always setting a correct key on a compacted topic matters, and why seeing null-keyed records disappear is expected given how compaction is defined.

Reason four is aggressive compaction settings. How quickly superseded records are removed depends on tunables. A small `segment.bytes` or short `segment.ms` rolls the active segment sooner so recent updates become eligible for cleaning quickly, a low `min.cleanable.dirty.ratio` makes the cleaner run even when only a small fraction of the log is stale, and a short cleaner backoff makes it run often. With all of these aggressive, an old value for a key can be purged almost immediately after a newer value is written. If you expected to still find a slightly older version for debugging or replay, it is already gone. That rapid removal is exactly what aggressive settings request, so it is expected behavior.

The unifying senior-level point is that compaction's guarantee is narrow and precise: it retains at least the latest value per key, subject to tombstone expiry, subject to any additional delete policy, only for properly keyed records, and on a schedule you control. Every case where data disappears is one of these rules operating as documented. The practical implications are: design consumers to treat null values as deletes so tombstone expiry does not leave them with stale state; choose compact versus compact,delete deliberately based on whether you want unbounded latest-per-key or bounded-plus-deduplicated; enforce non-null correct keys at the producer, ideally with a schema or validation, so nothing silently falls outside the compaction guarantee; and tune compaction aggressiveness to match how long you actually need superseded versions to remain, lengthening delete retention if slow consumers must observe deletes and relaxing the dirty ratio if you need older versions to survive longer. A subtle operational nuance is that because compaction runs per partition and lazily, the disappearance is also timing-dependent, so the same key may still be visible on one partition's uncleaned segment while gone from another, which again is expected given the lazy, partition-local cleaner.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India keeps account state in a compacted topic `account.state`, expecting the latest snapshot per account to always be available for cache rebuilds. Rajesh is SAV2001 and Priya is CUR3001. Over time, operators were surprised by data vanishing in four different ways and suspected bugs.

Problem 1 — after deleting a closed account with a tombstone, its key disappeared entirely a day later. Problem 2 — a topic mistakenly configured as compact plus delete expired the latest snapshot of a dormant account purely on age. Problem 3 — some events published with a null key vanished under retention while compaction never protected them. Problem 4 — on a topic with very aggressive compaction settings, the previous snapshot of an account was gone almost immediately after an update, breaking a debugging workflow that relied on the prior version. Each was actually documented behavior.

Our runnable demo models a `CompactedTopic` with a configurable policy and settings, and a `Cleaner` that applies all four rules, then shows each disappearance and labels it as expected with the governing setting. The classes are `CompactionDisappearanceDemo`, `Record`, `TopicConfig`, `CompactedTopic`, and `Cleaner`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four separate compacted topics, each configured to trigger one of the four disappearance reasons.

Step 1 (reason one): On a pure compact topic, we write a snapshot for SAV2001 then a tombstone. The cleaner runs twenty-five hours later. Because the tombstone is older than the twenty-four-hour delete retention, it is removed along with the key, so SAV2001 is entirely gone. The data disappeared exactly as the tombstone mechanism specifies.

Step 2 (reason two): On a compact plus delete topic with one-hour time retention, we write the latest snapshot for a dormant account and let two hours pass. The time-retention rule applies on top of compaction and removes the record despite it being the latest value for its key, because compact plus delete means both policies are in force. This is intended for bounded changelogs.

Step 3 (reason three): On a topic that allows deletion, we publish a record with a null key. Compaction cannot deduplicate it because there is no key, so it is governed only by retention, and after one hour it is deleted. It was never under the latest-per-key guarantee, so its disappearance is expected and is really a producer discipline problem.

Step 4 (reason four): On a topic with an aggressive dirty ratio and a tiny cleaner backoff, we write an old version then a new version for CUR3001. The cleaner runs almost immediately and removes the superseded old version at once. Anyone relying on finding the prior version for debugging finds it already gone, which is exactly what aggressive settings request.

Step 5: In every case the cleaner is doing precisely what its configuration specifies. The lesson is that compaction retains at least the latest value per key only within the bounds of tombstone expiry, any additional delete policy, correct keying, and the aggressiveness you configured, so each disappearance is documented behavior rather than a bug.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Log compaction guarantees that a compacted topic retains at least the latest value per key, but that guarantee is narrow and has four documented exceptions, so data disappearing is almost always compaction behaving exactly as specified rather than a bug. The first reason is the tombstone. You delete a key by producing a record with that key and a null value, and compaction keeps that tombstone only for the delete retention window, defaulting to twenty-four hours, so slow consumers can observe the delete. After that window and a cleaning pass, the tombstone and the key are gone entirely, which is the self-expiring delete marker working as designed.

The second reason is the cleanup policy. A topic set to compact only keeps the latest value per key forever, but a topic set to compact plus delete applies ordinary time or size retention on top of compaction, so even the latest value for a rarely updated key can expire purely on age. That is intended for a bounded, deduplicated changelog, and people are only surprised when they assumed compaction meant the latest value lives forever. The third reason is non-compactable records. Compaction is keyed, so a record with a null key or an accidentally wrong key is never under the latest-per-key guarantee and is governed only by retention, which means it can vanish while you thought compaction was protecting it. That is really a producer-discipline issue. The fourth reason is aggressive settings. Small segments, a low cleanable dirty ratio, and a short cleaner backoff make the cleaner remove superseded versions almost immediately, so an older version you hoped to still find for debugging is already gone, which is precisely what aggressive settings request.

On the National Bank of India account-state topic we chased all four of these as suspected bugs before realizing each was documented behavior. A closed account's key vanished a day after its tombstone, a dormant account's latest snapshot expired on a compact plus delete topic, some null-keyed events disappeared under retention, and on an aggressively tuned topic the previous snapshot was purged the instant a new one arrived.

The way I turn this understanding into correct design is concrete. I make every consumer treat a null value as a delete so tombstone expiry never leaves stale state behind. I choose compact versus compact plus delete deliberately, picking pure compact when I need an unbounded latest-per-key store and compact plus delete when I want deduplication with a time or size bound. I enforce non-null, correct keys at the producer, ideally with validation or a schema, so nothing silently falls outside the compaction guarantee. And I tune the aggressiveness, lengthening delete retention when slow consumers must observe deletes and relaxing the dirty ratio when I need older versions to survive longer. The one-line principle I give the team is that compaction keeps the latest value per key only within the bounds of tombstone expiry, any additional delete policy, correct keying, and the schedule you configured, so when data disappears, the first thing to check is the topic's exact configuration, not the code.

keyPoints: Retention: time-based (7 days default) or size-based
Compaction: keep latest value per key — delete old versions
Compacted topic: acts as a key-value snapshot store
